abstract.text: Normalizing flows are a powerful tool for building expressive distributions in high dimensions. So far, most of the literature has concentrated on learning flows on Euclidean spaces. Some problems however, such as those involving angles, are defined on spaces with more complex geometries, such as tori or spheres. In this paper, we propose and compare expressive and numerically stable flows on such spaces. Our flows are built recursively on the dimension of the space, starting from flows on circles, closed intervals or spheres.

predecessors.cited_work: Euclidean normalizing flow literature, including Papamakarios et al. (2019), Durkan et al. (2019b), Müller et al. (2019)

evidence.quote: Spline flows is a methodology for creating arbitrarily flexible flow transformations from R to itself, first proposed by Müller et al. (2019) and further developed by Durkan et al. (2019a; b).
For an overview of various implementations and associated trade-offs, see (Papamakarios et al., 2019).

predecessors.why: The paper builds on standard change-of-variables flow machinery and extends it to non-Euclidean manifolds.

predecessors.cited_work: Gemici et al. (2016) Riemannian manifold normalizing flows

evidence.quote: To circumvent this restriction, Gemici et al. (2016) first project M to RD, apply the usual flows there, and then project RD back to N.
Compact manifolds such as tori and spheres are not homeomorphic to RD, hence φ cannot be defined everywhere on M.

predecessors.why: The paper contrasts its direct compact-manifold constructions with projection-based Riemannian flow methods that can be numerically unstable.

predecessors.cited_work: Falorsi et al. (2019) Lie-group reparameterized distributions

evidence.quote: Another approach, proposed by Falorsi et al. (2019) for the case where N is a Lie group, is to apply the usual Euclidean flows on the Lie algebra of N (i.e. the tangent space at the identity element), and then use the exponential map to project the Lie algebra onto N.
The main drawbacks of this method is that the exponential map cannot be easily composed with other maps (since it is not generally bijective), and can be expensive to compute in high-dimensions.

predecessors.why: The paper contrasts its composable flows with Lie-algebra exponential-map methods whose maps are not easily composable.

evidence.quote: This motivates us to explore exponential-map flows, a mechanism for building flows on spheres proposed by Sei (2013).
We demonstrate substantial improvement relative to the polynomial scalar field, but we find that the exponential-map flow with either scalar field is not yet competitive with the recursive flow.

predecessors.why: The paper builds on Sei's exponential-map construction but improves the scalar field and finds it still less competitive than its recursive sphere flow.

predecessors.cited_work: Directional statistics, e.g. Mardia & Jupp (2009), Fisher (1953), and related distributions

evidence.quote: In general, the above three strategies lead to distributions with tractable density evaluation and sampling algorithms only in special cases, which typically yield simple distributions with limited flexibility.

Finally, we observe that the well-known von Mises–Fisher distribution on S2 (Fisher, 1953) can be obtained by transforming a uniform base density with Equations (12) to (14), where f is the identity and g has a simple functional form (for details, see Jakob, 2012).

predecessors.why: The paper positions its flows as more flexible than traditional directional-statistics distributions while connecting to known cases such as von Mises–Fisher.

abstract.text: Normalizing flows are a powerful tool for building expressive distributions in high dimensions. So far, most of the literature has concentrated on learning flows on Euclidean spaces. Some problems however, such as those involving angles, are defined on spaces with more complex geometries, such as tori or spheres. In this paper, we propose and compare expressive and numerically stable flows on such spaces. Our flows are built recursively on the dimension of the space, starting from flows on circles, closed intervals or spheres.

The main drawbacks of this method is that the exponential map cannot be easily composed with other maps (since it is not generally bijective), and can be expensive to compute in high-dimensions.
